title: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: most likely it will at some level be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than to set up some special version of human-like thinking only for specific tasks.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Human Thinking” (from p. 620), p. 629. Scope: artificial intelligence and emulation of human thinking

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-22: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Contemporary general and specialized systems provide relevant comparative evidence. However, the prediction concerns ease of reproduction at an unspecified level and bundles a separate claim about experience, so existing benchmarks resolve only proxies.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define comparable engineering budgets and benchmarks for broad human-like agents versus agents restricted to selected tasks, then compare development cost, sample efficiency, and performance, with and without human-like experience corpora. Lower cost for broad agents would support the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Human-like thinking has no agreed metric.

Current systems and benchmarks are selected by research incentives.

Historical engineering effort is not standardized.

fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.48
data existence: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.5

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Task-specific benchmarks and the public record of artificial systems give a partial, confounded comparison of narrow and broader aims. They do not measure 'general human-like thinking' on a scale that would cleanly show it is easier, and the further requirement of a human-like experience base is only loosely represented. The prediction is testable in part and not decided by current benchmarks.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the engineering cost and success of systems aimed at general human-like performance with systems aimed at declared specific tasks, and test whether human-like performance appears only after a human-like experience base. Systematically easier general systems would support the claim; systematically earlier and cheaper success on specific tasks would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
General human-like thinking has no single public score comparable to task benchmarks.

'Easier' depends on how tasks are chosen and on research effort, which is not an experimental control.
